"Teaching to the test" is a bit triggering for me.  

I started teaching college in 1985, and it was very important to me to be pretty strict about not doing that kind of thing--teaching to the test, providing make-work extra credit, writing multiple choice questions with one one answer that makes even the slightest sense--but not every teacher there was.  

And it really bothered me, because we often taught several sections of the same class.  At the end of the semester we got together to compare score distributions and decide where the letter grade boundaries were.

All sections had two common hour exams and a final exam.  All the profs teaching the sections contributed to writing these exams.  We did this several days before the test.  There was always a suspicion, especially with a couple of professors, that they would "teach to the test" in their section.

One of the reasons I left academia were issues like that, issues of basic fairness seemed so obvious and yet so hard to actually maintain.

So I went into software development for places like insurance companies and big box stores, where there were absolutely no problems whatsoever.

A (male) Roman citizen typically had three names; and Gaius Julius Caesar was an ordinary, concerned, citizen, not a king--no, no kings in Rome!

The second, the *nomen*, was the family, or really clan, name--passed down through the generations. And "Julius" was a pretty good one to have. 

Before that came the *praenomen*: there were about twenty in common use, of which "Gaius" was the most common--so common, in fact, that it was usually just abbreviated "C." Why "C" and not "G"? Just begause.

Finally one would have a *cognomen*, which was sort of a nickname--"Hairy" (Caesar) or "Chickpea" (Cicero). But even a cognomen could passed down within a family: the first hairy Julian was Sextus Julius Caesar, who played a role in the Second Punic War (early 3rd. c. BCE).

Where did the Romans get this system? Probably from the Etruscans. In any case, it wasn't the typical Indo-European system, in which a personal name would be unique, usually consisting of two parts: "Bran-wen," "Vladi-mir,"

You had me looking it up, and it seems that both versions are accepted, with Gaius being the more modern one.

The explanation for the two spellings is as follows:

"Early Latin: Early Roman writing used the letter C to write both the hard "k" sound and the "g" sound.
The Letter G: Romans later invented the letter G to tell the sounds apart.
Old Habits: Many traditional names kept the old spelling with a C out of habit. This is why his first name was still written with a C in official abbreviations like C. IVLIVS CAESAR."

Saying otherwise is like saying the decade of the Great Depression wasn't the 30s, because the stock market crashed in October, 1929. Another issue is when the conflict began being called "World War II." The NYT didn't use the term until after Pearl Harbor, and in fact, drawing the US into the conflict may have turned it from a series of regional conflicts into a true world war. Before that, many people just called it "the war," but some called it WWII from the start. Of course, people started talking about a theoretical WWII shortly after the Great War, i.e. WWI, ended. It can be difficult to pinpoint when a war becomes a world war. Today, there are some who believe that between US-Iraq, Russia-Ukraine, and Israel-Palestine, we're already into the beginnings of WWIII, but we just don't know for sure until we see how things play out. I sure hope not, but if that's so, we might not have to wait for AI to destroy us. Anyway, on the basis of any and all of these reasons, I think there's no problem to be found here. https://www.reddit.com/r/AskHistorians/comments/1l90dkq/how_soon_did_ww2_start_getting_called_ww2/
